Nvidia: board investigates CEO Jensen Huang after revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence

Nvidia's board of directors opened an independent investigation on Sunday, November 8, into its CEO, Jensen Huang, who admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom the Wall Street Journal describes as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Three House committee chairs want to hear from him on November 18 [1][2][3].

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia's board of directors announced an investigation led by its independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, into the ties between its CEO, Jensen Huang, and Alice Huang, an executive at the company Megaspeed [1][2].
The board says it has "no reason to believe" that national security or company secrets were compromised, and Nvidia confirms that Jensen Huang keeps his duties during the investigation [1][2].

In a message to staff, Jensen Huang admitted to an affair and promised to cooperate with the investigation [2]. The Wall Street Journal describes Alice Huang as a business executive believed to be a Chinese intelligence operative [3].

Three Republican chairs of House committees, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, are asking Jensen Huang for a closed-door briefing on November 18, with a reply expected before November 11, on Nvidia's safeguards against adversary powers [3][4].
Democrats, including Representative Seth Magaziner, are calling for further investigation and want Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify too [3].
Nvidia says its contacts with Megaspeed were ordinary business dealings, and the Chinese government denies spying on Nvidia [3].

Nvidia reports its fiscal third-quarter results on November 17 [6]. Analyst Dan Ives calls the affair a "black eye" for Jensen Huang and does not rule out his replacement depending on the investigation's findings [3].
Key point: a board investigation and a call from Congress targeting Nvidia's boss add a governance risk to a stock already shaken by the sell-off in chip stocks [1][3][5].

The stock is coming off a black week: on November 5, Nvidia, Micron and Intel plunged in a chip sell-off fueled by fears of a slowdown in data centers after the US election [5]. Nvidia nonetheless says the five big cloud companies plan about $1.3 trillion of spending next year, which supports its orders [6]. The affair therefore lands on ground where investors are already looking for reasons to doubt.

The stakes go beyond private life: the three lawmakers are asking about Nvidia's safeguards against adversary powers, in a sector where chips are at the heart of the rivalry between Washington and Beijing [3]. Democrats want to widen the inquiry up to the Commerce Secretary [3].

At this stage the board sees no compromise, but the findings could change the picture: Dan Ives raises a possible departure of the CEO depending on what the investigation shows, one more risk for the stock [3]. Two dates matter: November 11 for the reply to lawmakers, then the results on the 17th [4][6].

Nvidia designs the chips that run artificial intelligence; what affects its leadership can therefore shake the markets and the funds that hold its shares. For you, it is above all a reminder that a stock can move on a governance affair, not just on earnings. This is information, never advice to buy or sell.

How it works: key-person risk

When a company is closely identified with one person, investors speak of "key-person risk": if that person is implicated, replaced or distracted from their work, they fear that strategy and relationships with customers or governments will suffer. The board of directors, and in particular its independent members, is responsible for overseeing the CEO; it can launch an internal investigation with outside lawyers, then decide whether to keep, sanction or replace the executive. The share price then reflects two things: the probability that the executive leaves, and the confidence the market keeps in the company without them. A congressional inquiry does not sanction directly but can make customers, partners and authorities more cautious [1][3].
Precedents: executives who left over a relationship that broke company rules
June 2018
Brian Krzanich leaves the leadership of Intel after the disclosure of a past consensual relationship with an employee, in violation of the company's internal policy against such relationships [7].
A breached internal rule can be enough to remove a CEO even without financial wrongdoing; the board then acts on the executive's behavior, not on results [7].
September 1, 2025

Nestlé dismisses its chief executive, Laurent Freixe, after an investigation led by chairman Paul Bulcke and lead independent director Pablo Isla into an undisclosed romantic relationship with a direct subordinate; concerns had surfaced in the spring through an internal hotline, and he had at first denied it to the board. Philipp Navratil replaces him [8][9].
The board ran the investigation internally over several months, then decided: the executive lost his job and, according to the press, any severance package [8][9].

Anthropic prepares one of the biggest stock market listings in history, but with no price or date, just as the market doubts AI

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude assistant, filed on October 26 its registration to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. No price range has been published, and investors quoted in the press believe the targeted valuation, between $1.25 trillion and $2 trillion depending on the source, will have to come down after the sell-off in AI stocks [1][3][7][8].

On October 26, 2026, Anthropic made public its IPO filing with the US regulator (Form S-1): Class A shares listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead a syndicate of more than twenty banks [1][2].
On November 2, an amended version of the filing added third-quarter results: $17.0 billion in sales for July to September, more than 12 times the level a year earlier [3].
For the first half of 2026, the filing reports a net loss of $80.7 billion, mainly due to a $72.4 billion charge tied to changes in the fair value of convertible notes and other instruments [5][6].
The November 2 form leaves the price range blank ("between $ and $"); as of November 6, no new filing had appeared on the regulator's EDGAR database, according to a specialist tracker [7].

The valuation comes from the press, not from the filing: the Wall Street Journal mentions a raise of $100 billion or more for a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion; the Financial Times, $80 billion to $100 billion raised for $1.25 trillion to $1.75 trillion [7].

Several investors are already stepping back: one tells the Wall Street Journal the valuation will have to come down, another raises a complete postponement, a third talks about roughly $1 trillion [7][8].

The timetable remains unclear: according to The Information, the investor roadshow would begin the week of November 9; one estimate mentions first trades as early as November 16, another a listing before Thanksgiving, on November 26 [7].

Key point: an IPO turns a company financed by a few investors into one whose shares anyone can buy; here the scale is unprecedented, with up to $100 billion raised according to the press, against $75.0 billion for SpaceX, the current record [7][10].

The timing is delicate: on Thursday, November 5, Wall Street suffered a $2.5 trillion rout, fueled by fears that Democratic lawmakers would slow the rollout of the data centers that power AI [11]. An investor quoted by Yahoo Finance says Anthropic could postpone its IPO, another that it would come closer to $1 trillion [8].

The filing's numbers tell two stories: sales that more than grew twelvefold in a year ($17.0 billion in the third quarter) and a half-year loss of $80.7 billion, caused mostly by the revaluation of convertible notes rather than by day-to-day operations, which investors will examine line by line [3][5].

For the markets, the stakes are twofold: if the deal goes ahead, it will measure the real appetite for AI after this week's shock; if it is postponed, it will be one more sign of caution. No price is set: everything stays open until the range is published [7].

You probably will not be able to buy these shares at the IPO price: they are first reserved for large investors, then trade on the stock market. If you hold a US index fund, a company of this size could one day enter it. The most useful point: a valuation figure in the press is not a price, and an IPO can be postponed. How it works: an initial public offering

The company first files a public document with the regulator (Form S-1 in the United States) containing its accounts and its risks. It then adds a price range, and goes on a tour (the "roadshow") to present the deal to large investors. The banks leading the deal collect their orders, and the final price is set just before the first day of trading. The company's valuation is that price multiplied by the number of shares. On the first day, the price can move sharply away from the IPO price, in either direction. When the market tightens, the deal can be postponed: the price is never guaranteed until the company is listed [1][7].
Precedents: the biggest IPOs in history
May 2012
Facebook raises $16.0 billion in its IPO on May 17, 2012 [9].
An enormous amount at the time, now modest next to the $75.0 billion raised by SpaceX, the current record [9][10].
September 2014
Alibaba raises about $21.8 billion on the New York Stock Exchange on September 18, 2014 [9][10].
Third in the ranking of the biggest IPOs in history, behind Aramco and SpaceX [9][10].

Wendy's rejects the $1.4 billion offer from Nelson Peltz's fund and triggers a "poison pill" against a hostile takeover

On November 5, an independent committee of Wendy's board unanimously rejected the $7.35-per-share offer from a group led by Trian, Nelson Peltz's fund, which values the burger chain at about $1.4 billion. The company also adopted a one-year "poison pill" to prevent a takeover without its approval [1][2][5].

On October 28, a group made up of Trian Fund Management, BlueFive Capital, Sixth Street Partners and Flynn Group, one of the brand's largest franchisees, proposed $7.35 in cash per share to take Wendy's off the stock market [2][3].

The offer represented a premium of about 20% over the October 27 closing price and valued the equity at about $1.4 billion, on 194.0 million diluted shares [3][4]. The stock had jumped about 15% on the announcement [2].
Trian and its affiliates already hold about 16.3% of the capital, and Flynn Group operates more than 340 Wendy's restaurants [5].

On November 5, an independent committee of the board unanimously rejected the offer, judging that it undervalues the company's standalone prospects, and adopted a shareholder rights plan (the "poison pill") lasting one year [1][5].
Wendy's says the group refused a standstill agreement that would have frozen its additional share purchases [1][5].

The board points to the turnaround led by chief executive Bob Wright and the "Dave's Way" plan, announced with third-quarter results; the bidders reply that private ownership would give more time and resources to fix the company [5]. The stock has lost about 60% of its value in three years [2][3].
Another case of the same kind: Dine Brands, the parent of Applebee's and IHOP, recently rejected a $39-per-share proposal from Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital [5].
Key point: this is a classic test of strength, in which a shareholder that already owns 16.3% tries to buy the rest and the board refuses while protecting itself [1][5].

The pill's mechanism is simple: if an investor crosses a holding threshold without the board's approval, other shareholders can buy shares at a discount, which dilutes the attacker's stake and makes taking control very expensive. At Wendy's the duration is one year; the exact threshold does not appear in the sources consulted [5][6].

The two camps disagree on price: Wendy's judges that $7.35 undervalues the company and defends its turnaround plan, while the bidders argue that private ownership would save time; with a 60% drop in three years, the 20% premium does not erase the loss for those who bought higher [2][3][5].

The pill does not close the door: it gives the board time to negotiate a better price or defend its plan. It remains to be seen whether Trian raises its offer: it declined to comment on the rejection [5].

If you eat at Wendy's or work there, nothing changes in the short term: a takeover offer is not a closure or a layoff. For a shareholder, the "pill" does not say the offer is bad, but that the board wants a better price or to keep control. This is information, never advice to buy or sell.

How it works: the hostile bid and the "poison pill"

An offer is "hostile" when the target's board of directors rejects it. The buyer can then go directly to shareholders or buy shares on the market. To defend itself, the target can adopt a shareholder rights plan, the "poison pill": if someone crosses a holding threshold without approval, all other shareholders get the right to buy shares at a discount, which dilutes the attacker. The plan lasts one year here and does not prevent the board from negotiating or accepting an offer judged better. The attacker can challenge it in court, raise its price or try to replace the directors by gathering shareholders' votes. The proposed price, here $7.35, is compared with the market price: that is the "premium" [5][6].
Precedents: poison pills that held
April 2022
Twitter adopts a one-year pill, triggered if an investor buys more than 15% of the capital without the board's approval, when Elon Musk holds about 9% and has just proposed about $43 billion [6].
The pill did not close the door: the board noted it did not stop it from considering an offer it judged to be in shareholders' interest [6].
February 15, 2011

The Delaware Court of Chancery refuses to order Airgas to remove its pill against Air Products' "final" $70-per-share offer, which the board judges insufficient (it considers the company worth at least $78) [7][8].
A pill can be upheld to protect shareholders from an offer that is too low; after the ruling, Airgas stock fell more than 4%, to about $61 [7][8].
Only the Wendy's stock is directly concerned.

Australia: ANZ posts A$7.6 billion in profit, up 31%, but only up 10% excluding one-off items

Australian bank ANZ announced on Monday, November 9, a "cash" profit of A$7.6 billion for the year ended in September, up 31% and slightly above expectations. Excluding one-off items, the increase is only 10%, and the shares dipped slightly at the open [1][2][3].

On Monday, November 9, ANZ published a "cash" profit of A$7.6 billion (about US$5.2 billion) for the year ended September 30, up 31%, versus A$7.5 billion expected on average by analysts surveyed by Bloomberg [1][3].
Excluding one-off items ("significant items"), profit growth is only 10% [2][3].

Chief executive Nuno Matos attributes the result to "disciplined management of margins, capital and costs, and business growth"; he calls 2027 a "pivotal" year in which the plan will direct substantial funding toward growth initiatives [2].

The final dividend is 83 cents per share, 80% franked (covered by tax credits), up from 75% in the first half; over the year the total is A$1.66 per share, flat on a year earlier and slightly below expectations [2].
Matos notes that late repayments on home loans have ticked up [2].
The shares fell at Monday's open, by 0.5% to 1.5% depending on the source, despite a profit above expectations [2][3].

For comparison: in fiscal 2025, "cash" profit fell 14% to about A$5.79 billion, weighed down by A$1.1 billion of one-off items, including A$585 million for redundancies and A$271 million for a settlement with the regulator ASIC [4][5].
Key point: the +31% is mostly a comparison effect, because last year was weighed down by one-off costs; excluding one-off items, profit rises 10%, from about A$6.9 billion to A$7.6 billion [2][4].

A bank makes money mainly on the gap between what it pays depositors and what it charges borrowers (the margin), minus its costs and loan losses. That is why Nuno Matos talks about margins, capital and costs: these are the three levers of his plan, which he calls ANZ 2030 [2][4].

The point to watch comes from its customers: late repayments on home loans have ticked up, a sign that Australian households are under pressure. If arrears rose, the bank would have to set aside more money, which would reduce its profit [2].

The share dip despite a result above expectations shows the market was looking further ahead: a dividend slightly below forecasts and a 2027 presented as "pivotal" matter as much as last year's figure [2][3].

If you have an account, a loan or family in Australia, ANZ is one of the country's four big banks; its health matters for local mortgage lending. For a French reader, the example shows how to read a result: a spectacular percentage can hide a simple base effect. This is information, never advice to buy or sell.

How it works: "cash" profit and one-off items

When a bank publishes its results, it gives a "statutory" profit and a "cash" profit, the latter stripping out certain accounting items. It also lists "significant items": redundancy costs, fines, write-downs of holdings. Because they do not recur every year, growth is often compared with and without them. If the previous year contained many negative items, the headline increase looks very strong (+31%) while underlying growth is more modest (+10%). The dividend can be "franked": in Australia, tax already paid by the company is credited to the shareholder, which reduces their personal tax. Finally, the market judges results against analysts' expectations, not only against last year [2][4].
Precedents: ANZ between records and years weighed down by costs
November 2023
ANZ publishes a "cash" profit of A$7.405 billion for fiscal 2023, up 14% [6].
The A$7.4 billion level was already reached three years ago; the 2026 result only slightly exceeds it, which puts the +31% in perspective [6][1].
November 2025

For fiscal 2025, ANZ's "cash" profit fell 14% to about A$5.79 billion and statutory profit fell 10% to A$5.89 billion, with A$1.1 billion of one-off items: A$285 million for the write-down of PT Panin, A$585 million for redundancies, A$271 million for ASIC [4][5].
These one-off costs explain most of the 2025 drop and, in mirror image, of the 31% jump in 2026: excluding one-off items, profit had stayed stable at about A$6.9 billion [4][5].
Only ANZ is directly concerned.

Copper above $14,000 a tonne: Washington has not decided on tariffs, stocks flow to the United States and Shanghai pays a record

Copper is holding above $14,000 a tonne, near its September record ($14,875 on September 10, according to BMI), because the market is waiting for the US decision on tariffs targeting refined copper. More than 70% of LME stocks are already in US warehouses, and the spot premium in Shanghai is at a record [1][2].
According to BMI, copper hit a peak of $14,875 a tonne on September 10 and stayed well above $14,000 as of November 5 [1].
According to Shanghai Metals Market (SMM), more than 70% of London Metal Exchange (LME) copper stocks were in US warehouses as of November 5 [2].
On November 6, the premium paid for copper available immediately in Shanghai hit a record 2,615 yuan a tonne, a sign of tight supply and low local stocks, according to SMM [2].
The United States applies a 50% tariff on semi-finished copper products (Section 232); refined copper cathodes, concentrates, anodes and scrap have remained outside it [3].

The Commerce Department was due to report before June 30, 2026 on a phased tariff on refined copper: 15% from January 1, 2027, then 30% from January 1, 2028; BMI notes that the decision is still awaited in early November [1][3].
On the market balance, ING expects a deficit of about 35,000 tonnes in 2026, while the firm CRU, which had forecast a surplus, now judges the market at best balanced [4].
Key point: the copper price depends as much on a decision in Washington as on the balance between mines and factories, and until it is made, traders hedge [1][3].

The mechanism: if a tariff is to hit imported refined copper, metal sold in the United States is worth more than LME metal. Traders therefore ship copper to US warehouses before the deadline, which drains the rest of the world: LME stocks pile up in the United States and buyers elsewhere, as in Shanghai, pay a premium to get delivery [1][2].

The 2025 precedent shows the decision can move prices abruptly: US copper jumped more than 13% on July 8, 2025, then fell about 20% on July 30 when refined copper was excluded from the 50% tariff [5][6][7].

If Washington confirms the 15% tariff in 2027, US stocks could stay high; if it drops it, the premium could fall back. That is why the market stays suspended on the announcement, with no sign of a date in the sources consulted [1][3].

Copper is used in electric cables, motors, grids and charging stations: expensive copper ends up, with a delay, in the price of equipment and energy renovation. For a French reader, the effect is indirect and slow, but it shows how a US tariff shifts stocks and prices all over the world. This is information, never advice to buy or sell.

How it works: why a tariff moves copper stocks

Copper trades on two major venues: the LME in London, the global benchmark, and Comex in New York. Normally their prices stay close. When the United States announces or lets a tariff on imported copper loom, metal deliverable in the United States is worth more than LME metal: traders profit by shipping it to US warehouses before the tariff applies. US stocks swell, which removes metal available elsewhere. Buyers in the rest of the world, such as Chinese smelters, then have to pay a "premium" to get immediate delivery: that is the one hitting a record in Shanghai. If the US decision is cancelled or clarified, the gap closes and prices can drop sharply [1][2][6].
Precedents: copper shaken by US announcements in 2025
July 8, 2025
US copper (Comex) jumps more than 13% in one session, above $12,445 a tonne, a record, after the announcement of a 50% tariff on imported copper [5].
The announcement of a tariff lifts the US price even before it applies, because the market anticipates the local shortage [5].
The White House excludes refined copper from the 50% tariff: US copper falls about 20%, the biggest one-day drop ever recorded, from $5.59 to $4.35 a pound according to ING [6][7].
When the exemption falls away, the US premium evaporates at once, but Commerce recommended a deferred tariff of 15% in 2027 then 30% in 2028, which renews the wait [6][7].

Suzhou Denglin Technology, which designs graphics processing units (GPUs) for artificial intelligence, is due to debut on Tuesday, November 10 on the Hong Kong stock exchange (code 09917), with a range of HK$231 to HK$288 per share and up to HK$1.76 billion to raise. How it works: a Hong Kong IPO with "cornerstone investors"

Before opening the offer to the public, a company listing on the Hong Kong exchange can sign "cornerstone investors": large funds commit to buying a set number of shares at the final price, and to holding them for a period. This commitment reassures other buyers and helps set the price. The offer is split into a tranche for institutions and a tranche for the public (the "retail" tranche), whose subscription rate, meaning how many times it is covered, gives an idea of market appetite. The final price is set within the announced range, then shares start trading on listing day. An "H" share is a share of a mainland China company listed in Hong Kong [1][2][7].

South Korea: the Kospi gained 1.5% to 5,137.22 points, after falling about 6% on Friday; Tokyo's index had also lost about 6% that day [2].
The MSCI Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan rose 0.8%, after a 4.6% fall the previous week; in Hong Kong, the Hang Seng gained 0.2% to 24,525.58 points [1][2].

The origin is on Wall Street: on Thursday, November 5, $2.5 trillion of market value went up in smoke, over fears that a Democratic-majority Congress would slow the rollout of AI data centers; the S&P 500 had lost 4.4% and the Dow Jones more than 1,800 points [1][3].

On Friday, November 6, Wall Street rebounded on tech: the Nasdaq gained 1.1% to 24,579.42 points and the S&P 500 0.3% to 7,376.86, but the Dow Jones fell 0.5% to 51,285.73; over the week, the S&P 500 lost about 2.7% and the Nasdaq about 3.4% [3][4].
In Europe, the Stoxx 600 ended Friday down 1.0% at 648.33 points [5]. Attention turns to US inflation for October, due on November 10 [2].
Key point: this rebound is relief more than a reversal; analysts describe a modest recovery that follows Wall Street rather than leading it [1][2].

Asian stock markets are heavily exposed to chips: Tokyo Electron, Advantest and TSMC weigh heavily in their indexes, and they are the ones that had fallen the most. When fears about data-center spending ease a little, these stocks rebound the hardest [1][2].

The week's shock started from US politics: the election gave Congress a Democratic majority, and investors feared a brake on the data centers that run AI, a sector that has been boosting stock markets for months [1][3]. A new element weighed early in the session: the announcement of the investigation into Nvidia's CEO [2].
Caution remains in order: US inflation for October, published on November 10, can revive or calm fears about Fed rates; Asia-Pacific excluding Japan had just lost 4.6% the previous week [2].

If you have a global fund, a retirement savings plan or shares, this rebound softens last week without erasing it: the open in Europe and on Wall Street will show whether the calm holds. For a French reader, remember that the Taiwanese or Tokyo stock markets depend on chips, and therefore on the spending of the US cloud giants. This is information, never advice to buy or sell.
